logbook_fact: bowfin can gulp air at the surface when warm backwaters run low on oxygen. a long dorsal fin ripples as they stalk prey.
lake sturgeon sweep the bottom with four sensitive barbels before extending a tube-like mouth to feed. they can live for decades.
longnose gar wait near the surface before snapping sideways at passing fish. their narrow jaws carry rows of fine needle-like teeth.
paddlefish cruise open rivers with their mouths wide, filtering tiny plankton from the water. the broad snout senses faint electrical signals.
shovelnose sturgeon hug flowing river bottoms and probe for insect larvae. a flattened snout helps them hold position in strong current.
spotted gar linger among vegetation where their mottled bodies break up their outline. they rise to gulp air as well as breathing through gills.
west african lungfish breathe air with paired lungs. when floodplains dry, they seal themselves in a mud cocoon until water returns.
atlantic mudskippers use sturdy fins to hop and crawl across exposed mud. moist skin and mouth linings let them breathe out of water.
largescale foureyes cruise with each eye divided across the waterline. one half watches above while the other scans below.
red mullet comb sandy bottoms with two chin barbels that taste hidden prey. their foraging leaves winding trails in the sediment.
european plaice lie flat on the seafloor with both eyes on the same side. orange spots help distinguish them from neighboring flatfish.
summer flounder bury themselves in sand with only their eyes exposed. a sudden burst carries them upward to seize passing prey.
winter flounder favor cool bays and estuaries where they rest on muddy bottoms. their eyes sit on the right side of the body.
dugongs graze seagrass meadows with a downturned, bristled snout. they are the only fully marine members of the sirenian family.
harbor seals rest on rocky shores and sandbars between hunting trips. sensitive whiskers can trace the water trails left by moving fish.
sea otters float on their backs while opening shellfish with stones. dense fur traps insulating air because they lack a thick blubber layer.
walruses sweep the seafloor for clams and other soft-bodied prey. long tusks help them haul onto ice and settle disputes.
west indian manatees graze aquatic plants in warm coastal water and rivers. they surface regularly to breathe through nostrils atop the snout.
bay pipefish hide upright among seagrass, matching the blades with their slender bodies. males carry developing eggs in a brood pouch.
lined seahorses anchor to grass and coral with curling tails. the male broods eggs in a pouch and releases fully formed young.
monkfish hide against the bottom and wave a fleshy lure above a cavernous mouth. a sudden gulp draws fish and crustaceans inward.
tripletail often drift sideways near floating debris, resembling a loose leaf. rounded rear fins create the three-tailed silhouette.
atlantic mackerel travel in fast schools across the north atlantic and feed on plankton and small schooling fish.
bluefish race in coordinated schools while pursuing smaller fish. sharp teeth and powerful jaws make their feeding bursts especially fierce.
cero mackerel are streamlined coastal hunters. sharp teeth help them slash through schools of smaller fish.
chub mackerel school near the surface and follow plankton blooms. their dark wavy bars help identify them at a glance.
crevalle jacks patrol warm coasts in fast-moving schools. their deep bodies and forked tails deliver long, powerful runs.
king mackerel are swift coastal predators. their pointed teeth and long body are built for sudden bursts of speed.
spanish mackerel hunt in warm coastal waters and often travel in loose schools while chasing baitfish.
talang queenfish chase schooling prey near warm coasts and estuaries. hooked teeth and a deeply forked tail suit their rapid attacks.
american sand lance dive headfirst into loose sand when danger approaches. immense schools carry energy from plankton to larger predators.
atlantic menhaden strain plankton from coastal water with fine gill rakers. dense schools feed whales, seabirds, and predatory fish.
black pomfret have a deep, laterally compressed body that lets them maneuver neatly through open water.
chinese pomfret are silvery schooling fish with a tall, flattened body and long sickle-shaped fins.
european anchovies form dense schools and feed by filtering tiny plankton from coastal water.
european pilchards form shimmering schools along atlantic and mediterranean coasts. they feed mainly on plankton near the surface.
golden pomfret are warm-water swimmers whose golden sheen is most noticeable along the fins and flanks.
northern anchovies gather in huge schools along the pacific coast and filter plankton with their fine gill rakers.
pacific sardines follow cool, productive water in enormous schools. their movements shift as currents and plankton supplies change.
white pomfret gather over coastal grounds and use their compact, deep bodies to turn quickly while feeding.
blacktip sharks are named for the dark markings on their fins. they hunt schooling fish in warm shallows and sometimes leap clear of the water.
great hammerheads sweep their wide heads over the bottom while searching for rays. widely spaced senses help pinpoint hidden prey.
great white sharks conserve heat in their swimming muscles while crossing cool seas. rows of serrated teeth are replaced throughout life.
tiger sharks carry dark vertical bars that fade as they mature. broad jaws let them investigate an unusually varied range of prey.
whale sharks are enormous filter feeders covered in unique spot patterns. they cruise with open mouths to collect plankton and tiny fish.
burbot are the only freshwater members of the cod family. they become most active in cold darkness and may spawn beneath winter ice.
cisco school in the cool open water of northern lakes. these slim relatives of salmon feed on plankton and become prey for larger fish.
lake whitefish browse deep, cold bottoms with small downward-pointing mouths. large schools move toward shallows to spawn in autumn.
arctic char thrive farther north than any other freshwater fish. some remain in lakes while others migrate between rivers and the sea.
arctic grayling carry a tall, colorful dorsal fin like a sail. they feed on drifting insects in cold, clear rivers and lakes.
brown trout often shelter by day and hunt more freely after dark. adaptable populations occupy streams, lakes, and even coastal water.
cutthroat trout take their name from the red slash beneath the jaw. many populations rely on cold, well-oxygenated streams.
golden trout evolved in clear, high-elevation california streams. their bright flanks stand out against rocky alpine water.
rainbow trout are adaptable stream hunters. the pink lateral stripe is especially vivid when the fish is in breeding condition.
atlantic wolffish use heavy jaws and blunt teeth to crush shellfish and urchins. natural antifreeze proteins help them endure icy water.
cusk move slowly across cold rocky bottoms, sheltering in cracks and caves. a single long fin runs around much of the rear body.
spotted wolffish crush hard-shelled prey with broad molar-like teeth. their pale spots stand out against a dark cold-water body.
atlantic herring gather in immense schools that move between feeding and spawning grounds. they filter plankton with fine gill rakers.
capelin are small polar fish that feed whales, seabirds, and larger fish. many schools roll onto beaches or shallows to release their eggs.
european sprat form compact schools in northern coastal seas. these tiny herring relatives feed on plankton near the surface.
pacific herring return to coastal shallows to coat plants and rocks with eggs. their oily schools support entire marine food webs.
alaska pollock form vast schools over cold northern shelves. they feed on plankton and fish while supporting many larger predators.
atlantic cod carry a pale lateral line and one chin barbel. they search cold seafloors for crustaceans, mollusks, and smaller fish.
atlantic pollock are swift relatives of cod with dark backs and pale lateral lines. adults gather around rocky banks and wrecks.
dover sole glide over deep muddy bottoms of the eastern pacific. both eyes migrate to the right side as the young fish becomes flat.
haddock are recognized by a dark shoulder mark and black lateral line. schools forage over cold seafloors for small bottom animals.
pacific cod use a chin barbel to investigate cold shelf bottoms. seasonal schools follow prey between deeper water and coastal spawning grounds.
pacific hake rise from deep water at night to feed on krill and fish. large schools migrate along the west coast with changing seasons.
silver hake hunt fish and crustaceans over sandy atlantic shelves. they move upward after dark and return toward the bottom by day.
chambered nautiluses regulate buoyancy with gas-filled shell chambers. dozens of small tentacles feel for food in dark reef slopes.
common cuttlefish flash changing colors and patterns through specialized skin cells. an internal cuttlebone controls buoyancy.
flamboyant cuttlefish walk along the seafloor on their arms and fins. vivid displays warn predators of potent toxins.
blueline tilefish shelter in burrows and rocky openings along deep shelves. a narrow blue stripe traces the edge of the dorsal fin.
golden tilefish excavate burrows in soft clay along deep ocean slopes. their bright yellow spots contrast with blue-green backs.
pacific ocean perch hover around deep rocky reefs in the north pacific. these slow-growing fish give birth to live young.
patagonian toothfish patrol cold, deep southern water with large canine teeth. natural antifreeze proteins protect their blood from freezing.
sablefish roam deep north pacific slopes and can live for many decades. soft dark bodies conceal rich, oil-filled flesh.
wreckfish gather around caves, ledges, and shipwrecks in deep water. powerful jaws let them ambush fish and large crustaceans.
giant oarfish drift vertically through deep open water, rowing with a crimson dorsal fin. their ribbon-like bodies can reach remarkable lengths.
west indian ocean coelacanths shelter in deep volcanic caves by day. fleshy lobed fins move in an alternating, limb-like rhythm.
black seadevils lure prey with a glowing organ suspended above the mouth. tiny males permanently attach to much larger females.
common fangtooths carry outsized teeth that fit into pockets in the roof of the mouth. they migrate upward from deep water after dark.
gulper eels unfold enormous mouths to engulf prey in the deep sea. a whip-like tail ends in a small light-producing organ.
pacific barreleyes peer upward through transparent shields covering the head. tubular eyes rotate forward when the fish turns to feed.
smooth-head blobfish rest on deep slopes where pressure supports their soft bodies. they conserve energy by waiting for edible matter nearby.
spotted lanternfish carry rows of light-producing organs along their bodies. immense schools rise toward the surface each night.
crown-of-thorns sea stars crawl over reefs and digest coral tissue outside the body. venomous spines discourage many predators.
giant california sea cucumbers sweep organic particles from the seafloor with branching tentacles. soft tube feet anchor their long bodies.
purple sea urchins scrape algae from rocks with a five-toothed feeding structure. dense groups can clear kelp from entire reefs.
sand dollars burrow just beneath sandy seafloors and filter tiny food particles. the familiar star pattern marks their five-part body plan.
sunflower sea stars move quickly on thousands of tube feet and may carry many arms. they hunt urchins, clams, and other bottom animals.
axolotls remain aquatic and keep feathery external gills throughout adulthood. lost limbs and parts of several organs can regenerate.
hellbenders hide beneath large rocks in cool, clean rivers. folds of loose skin absorb oxygen while the flattened body grips the current.
guppies are livebearers whose young arrive ready to swim. males display bright colors while females often favor larger, less flashy bodies.
neon tetras school through shaded forest streams. an iridescent blue stripe remains visible in the dim, tannin-stained water.
zebrafish carry horizontal blue stripes from gill to tail. hardy schools thrive in shallow streams, flooded fields, and quiet pools.
largemouth bass wait among weeds and timber before lunging at prey. the upper jaw extends beyond the eye when the mouth is closed.
smallmouth bass favor clear water with rock and moving current. bronze flanks and dark vertical bars distinguish them from largemouth bass.
bigmouth buffalo filter plankton with fine gill rakers instead of rooting for prey. some individuals survive for more than a century.
golden redhorses probe flowing river bottoms with fleshy, downward-facing mouths. coppery scales and reddish fins give them a warm glow.
quillbacks carry a long first dorsal ray that rises like a quill. small mouths gather insect larvae and other food from river and lake bottoms.
smallmouth buffalo use thick lips to graze bottom-dwelling food in warm rivers. their deep, heavy bodies form a pronounced arch behind the head.
white suckers vacuum insects and organic matter from cool freshwater bottoms. spring runs carry large groups into shallow streams.
black bullheads tolerate warm, cloudy water with little oxygen. stout spines protect the dorsal and pectoral fins from predators.
a deep fork in the tail inspired the blue catfish's scientific name. it rests deep by daylight and becomes more active after dark.
brown bullheads search muddy bottoms with eight sensitive barbels. males guard nests and herd newly hatched young in a dark moving ball.
a channel catfish can taste through skin all over its body, especially near its gills and whiskers. the male watches the eggs.
flatheads favor hideouts made by logs, rocks, ledges, and other underwater structure. as they grow, fish dominate their menu.
tadpole madtoms are tiny nocturnal catfish that shelter beneath vegetation and debris. venomous fin spines discourage larger predators.
white catfish began along the atlantic coast between new york and florida. people later carried them far beyond that home range.
yellow bullheads use pale chin barbels to distinguish food in murky shallows. both parents may guard the nest and schooling young.
common barbels hold close to fast river bottoms with streamlined bodies and broad fins. four mouth barbels locate food among stones.
common bream gather in slow rivers and lakes with silvery, deep-sided bodies. protruding mouths sift insect larvae from soft bottoms.
whisker-like barbels help a common carp investigate the bottom. nosing through sediment can cloud the water and loosen plants.
common roach thrive in many lakes and rivers, often schooling near vegetation. red fins and a red-orange eye brighten their silver bodies.
european chub are adaptable river fish. adults often patrol shallows and feed on insects, small fish, and fruit.
fallfish are large minnows that build broad stone nests in flowing water. other stream fish often reuse the gravel mounds for spawning.
ide move between rivers, lakes, and brackish coastal water in loose schools. adults eat insects, crustaceans, plants, and small fish.
rudd feed near the surface with an upturned mouth and red fins. golden-green bodies disappear easily among warm, weedy shallows.
tench browse quiet, muddy bottoms with two small mouth barbels. a thick coat of slime protects their olive-green scales.
red swamp crayfish burrow into wet ground when water recedes. adaptable populations feed on plants, carrion, and small aquatic animals.
alligator gar combine a broad tooth-filled snout with heavy armor-like scales. a vascular swim bladder lets them breathe air at the surface.
arapaima must surface frequently to gulp air through a specialized swim bladder. large armored scales protect their long river-going bodies.
goliath tigerfish patrol powerful african rivers with interlocking dagger-like teeth. a muscular forked tail drives sudden attacks.
muskellunge wait motionless among weeds before exploding toward prey. pale bodies carry bars or spots that fade into broken underwater light.
common shiners flash silver in clear streams and small rivers. breeding males develop rosy fins and a blue-violet sheen.
creek chubs gather around pools and undercut banks in small streams. males build gravel ridges where several fish may spawn.
emerald shiners form bright surface schools in large lakes and rivers. slender bodies feed on plankton and drifting insects.
fathead minnows tolerate warm, muddy ponds where many fish struggle. males guard eggs laid beneath rocks, logs, and other cover.
flame chubs prefer cool, clear streams. their bright breeding colors make a small fish easy to spot in spring water.
golden shiners school around dense vegetation in warm water. an upturned mouth takes insects and plankton from near the surface.
lake chubs school in cold northern water and use their small mouths to pick insects and other tiny prey from the current.
electric eels navigate and hunt with electrical pulses produced along most of the body. they must surface regularly to breathe air.
freshwater drum crush snails and mussels with powerful throat teeth. muscles vibrating against the swim bladder produce a low drumming sound.
goldeye patrol turbid rivers with large light-sensitive eyes and a toothed tongue. they rise toward the surface to hunt insects and small fish.
mooneyes flash silver in clear rivers and lakes while feeding near the surface. their large eyes suit evening hunts for insects and small fish.
weather loaches gulp air and pass it through the intestine when oxygen runs low. restless activity often increases as air pressure falls.
bubble-eye goldfish have delicate fluid-filled sacs beneath their eyes, making careful handling especially important.
goldfish can tolerate a surprisingly wide range of conditions. their wild relatives often live in slow, weedy water.
koi are colorful domesticated forms of common carp selected over many generations. each fish carries a distinctive arrangement of patches and scales.
black crappie gather around submerged wood and vegetation in clear water. irregular dark speckles scatter across their deep silver bodies.
bluegill fathers sweep shallow bowls into the bottom for nests, then stand guard. whole neighborhoods of nests can crowd together.
green sunfish tolerate small, warm, cloudy pools better than many relatives. a large mouth lets them tackle insects, crayfish, and fish.
pumpkinseeds use compact teeth to crush snails and other hard prey. blue facial lines and an orange gill spot brighten their round bodies.
redear sunfish specialize in snails, crushing shells with strong throat teeth. a red or orange margin marks the dark flap behind the gill.
warmouth hide in weeds, roots, and murky backwaters before ambushing prey. red eyes and dark cheek stripes frame a notably large mouth.
white crappie favor warm, cloudy water and gather around structure. vertical bars cross their silver sides instead of scattered speckles.
yellow perch travel in schools through cool lakes and slow rivers. dark vertical bars and orange lower fins make them easy to recognize.
chain pickerel hover among vegetation before darting at fish and frogs. a chain-like pattern breaks up their green flanks.
grass pickerel remain small enough to hunt in narrow, weedy creeks and marshes. dark bars camouflage their slim bodies among stems.
northern pike are solitary ambush hunters built for sudden acceleration. pale bean-shaped spots cover their long green bodies.
sauger favor turbid rivers and reservoirs. their mottled backs blend into the dim, shifting light near the bottom.
saugeye are a fertile hybrid of sauger and walleye. they combine traits from both parent species and often grow quickly.
walleye have light-sensitive eyes that help them hunt in murky water and around dusk. their reflective layer gives the eyes a pale glow.
round gobies use fused pelvic fins like a suction cup to hold onto rocks. they are small fish with a famously large appetite.
crystal jellies are nearly transparent except for glowing points around the bell. their green fluorescent protein transformed biological research.
lion's mane jellies trail dense curtains of tentacles through cold seas. the bell darkens from yellow to deep red as the animal grows.
moon jellies pulse gently with four horseshoe-shaped organs visible through the bell. short tentacles sweep plankton toward the mouth.
pacific sea nettles carry rust-colored stripes across pale bells. long tentacles and frilled mouth arms capture plankton and small fish.
sea wasps have box-shaped bells and clusters of eyes along the lower edge. their long tentacles deliver exceptionally potent venom.
african pompano develop long streaming fin rays while young. adults become deep-bodied silver hunters around reefs and offshore structure.
cobia often follow sharks, rays, and floating structures in warm seas. a broad dark stripe runs along their long, powerful bodies.
giant trevally hunt reef edges with bursts of speed and force. large individuals sometimes charge prey from surf and shallow lagoons.
greater amberjacks circle reefs, wrecks, and offshore platforms. a dark stripe crosses the eye of their sturdy torpedo-shaped bodies.
lesser amberjacks school around deep reefs and floating objects. an enlarged eye suits their preference for dimmer water.
atlantic halibut are immense right-eyed flatfish of cold northern seas. adults ambush fish and squid from deep rocky or sandy bottoms.
pacific halibut lie camouflaged on cold continental shelves. powerful flat bodies can travel long distances between feeding and spawning grounds.
turbot have broad, nearly circular bodies covered with bony bumps instead of scales. they bury into sand before ambushing fish and crustaceans.
american lobsters shelter in rocky crevices and emerge to forage along the bottom. one claw crushes while the other cuts and grips.
antarctic krill form enormous swarms beneath southern seas and ice. these small crustaceans feed whales, seals, penguins, and fish.
caribbean spiny lobsters rely on long antennae and a thorny shell instead of large claws. groups march together across the seafloor.
peacock mantis shrimp strike hard-shelled prey with club-like limbs. complex eyes move independently and detect colors beyond human vision.
skunk cleaner shrimp advertise at reef cleaning stations with bright white antennae. visiting fish pause while parasites are picked away.
atlantic ghost crabs dash across beaches on long pale legs and retreat into deep burrows. raised eyes scan nearly every direction.
blue crabs swim with flattened rear legs shaped like paddles. bright blue claws and an olive shell conceal a quick, defensive temperament.
dungeness crabs bury beneath sand with only their eyes and antennae exposed. broad toothed shells protect them along cool pacific coasts.
japanese spider crabs carry the longest leg span of any living arthropod. adults roam deep seafloors around japan.
red king crabs stride over cold northern bottoms on long armored legs. despite the name, they are closer to hermit crabs than true crabs.
american eels hatch far out in the sargasso sea before entering freshwater rivers. adults later reverse the journey to spawn once.
european eels cross the atlantic as transparent larvae before entering rivers and lakes. mature silver eels return to sea to reproduce.
rainbow smelt move between coastal water and rivers, though some remain landlocked. cucumber-like aromas cling to freshly caught fish.
eulachon return from the pacific to spawn in coastal rivers. their oil-rich bodies once served as candles when dried and fitted with wicks.
white sturgeon are the largest freshwater fish in north america. armored plates line bodies built for long lives in rivers and estuaries.
atlantic salmon can return from the ocean to the river where they hatched. unlike many salmon, some survive to make the trip again.
chum salmon travel immense distances and develop striking bars when they return to fresh water to spawn.
coho salmon are agile hunters known for powerful leaps. young coho may spend more than a year growing in streams.
pink salmon usually follow a strict two-year life cycle. spawning males develop the hump that inspired their nickname.
sockeye salmon feed heavily on plankton at sea. adults turn vivid red as they return inland to spawn.
steelhead are the ocean-going form of rainbow trout. adults can leave fresh water and later return to spawn.
black marlin are powerful billfish that spend much of their lives in warm open ocean and can make blistering runs.
blue marlin are highly migratory open-ocean hunters. their long bill helps them stun prey before turning back to feed.
sailfish raise their enormous dorsal fin while herding baitfish. they are among the fastest fish in the sea.
swordfish are fast, wide-ranging predators with a flattened bill. they can cross deep water and warm surface layers in one day.
white marlin favor warm offshore water and use their rounded dorsal fin and bill to weave through schools of prey.
mahi-mahi flash brilliant blue, green, and gold while chasing prey near the surface. they grow quickly and gather around floating objects.
opah circulate warm blood through much of the body, an unusual trait among fish. round silver flanks glow with red fins and pale spots.
wahoo are streamlined open-ocean hunters with rows of sharp teeth. blue vertical bars flicker across their sides during fast pursuits.
albacore have unusually long pectoral fins. their warm muscles help them cruise across wide stretches of open ocean.
bigeye tuna make daily trips between deep, cool water and warmer surface layers. their large eyes suit those dim depths.
bluefin tuna are powerful ocean travelers. heat retained in their swimming muscles lets them thrive in surprisingly cold seas.
skipjack travel in fast-moving schools and have dark stripes along their lower sides. they rarely stop swimming.
yellowfin are named for their bright yellow fins and finlets. large schools often gather with other open-ocean hunters.
common octopuses squeeze through narrow cracks and solve problems while hunting reefs. skin cells rapidly change color and texture.
day octopuses forage across tropical reefs while the sun is high. shifting bars and spots communicate alarm, camouflage, and threat.
giant pacific octopuses explore cold rocky dens with thousands of arm suckers. females guard their eggs without feeding until they hatch.
greater blue-ringed octopuses reveal vivid rings when threatened. a tiny beak can deliver venom strong enough to stop breathing.
ocean sunfish are built more like enormous swimming heads than ordinary fish. they visit the surface and turn sideways to warm up.
barndoor skates glide over cold atlantic bottoms with broad wing-like fins. rows of thorny spines protect the back and tail.
giant manta rays funnel plankton into wide mouths with two flexible head fins. each belly carries a unique pattern of dark spots.
largetooth sawfish detect hidden prey with a long sensory rostrum. a swift sideways sweep stuns fish and exposes animals buried in mud.
ocellate river stingrays carry bright eye-like spots across a round disc. they hide beneath sand in south american rivers.
southern stingrays bury in warm sand with only their eyes and spiracles visible. crushing plates break open clams and crustaceans.
red lionfish spread ornate venomous spines when threatened. broad fins herd smaller fish into corners before a rapid gulp.
red scorpionfish vanish against rocky reefs through mottled color and skin flaps. venomous dorsal spines punish careless predators.
green morays appear green because yellow mucus coats blue-gray skin. a second set of jaws pulls captured prey deeper into the throat.
peacock flounders change their spots and colors to match tropical sand. both eyes scan above while the flat body remains concealed.
blue tangs graze algae from coral reefs with small close-set teeth. sharp folding spines near the tail give surgeonfish their name.
rainbow parrotfish scrape algae from reefs with fused beak-like teeth. crushed coral passes through them and returns to the reef as sand.
stoplight parrotfish change color dramatically as they mature. powerful dental plates bite algae from hard reef surfaces.
yellow tangs browse algae across hawaiian reefs during daylight. at night their bright bodies darken and show a pale horizontal stripe.
atlantic trumpetfish hover head-down among corals and sea fans. long tubular snouts expand suddenly to draw in small fish.
gray triggerfish lock a stout dorsal spine upright when wedged into shelter. strong teeth crack barnacles, crabs, and shellfish.
guineafowl puffers swallow water to inflate when threatened. adults may shift from a spotted dark pattern to a vivid yellow form.
longhorn cowfish wear a rigid box of fused scales with horns above the eyes. small fins steer the angular body with surprising precision.
queen triggerfish blow jets of water to uncover buried prey and flip sea urchins. vivid blue lines radiate across the face.
red cornetfish stalk reefs with extremely long bodies and tubular snouts. a trailing filament extends from the center of the tail.
spotted porcupinefish inflate until long spines stand outward. fused teeth form a strong beak for crushing shelled prey.
yellow boxfish juveniles are bright cubes covered in black spots. rigid body armor leaves small fins to provide careful steering.
copperband butterflyfish probe reef cracks with long narrow snouts. bold orange bands and a false eyespot confuse predators.
ocellaris clownfish shelter safely among stinging anemone tentacles. each group is led by a female that develops from the largest male.
queen angelfish graze sponges from warm atlantic reefs. a blue-ringed spot on the forehead resembles a tiny crown.
atlantic goliath groupers occupy reefs, wrecks, and mangrove roots. enormous mouths pull prey inward with a sudden pressure drop.
bluefin trevally hunt reef fish in coordinated groups. electric blue fins and scattered blue spots contrast with a golden body.
giant groupers become massive ambush predators around indo-pacific reefs. juveniles carry bold black-and-yellow markings.
great barracudas hover motionless before accelerating toward prey. long jaws carry two distinct rows of sharp teeth.
gulf grouper are ambush predators that use a sudden gulp to pull prey into their cavernous mouths.
nassau groupers shift their bars and colors with mood and surroundings. adults gather at traditional reef sites to spawn.
red grouper excavate shelters in reef rubble. the hollows they make can become hiding places for many smaller animals.
blue-green chromis form loose clouds above branching coral. the school dives into narrow shelter whenever a predator approaches.
bluestriped grunts shelter on reefs by day and spread over seagrass to feed at night. grinding throat teeth produce audible grunts.
french grunts gather in yellow-striped schools around reefs and wrecks. they travel into nearby sand and grass beds after dark.
sergeant majors guard purple egg patches on hard reef surfaces. five dark bars cross their yellow and silver bodies.
lane snapper use reef structure for cover and hunt small crustaceans and fish when the light begins to fade.
mangrove snapper shelter among roots and docks when young, then move toward reefs as they grow.
mutton snapper have canine teeth that help them pick crabs, shrimp, and other hard-shelled prey from the reef.
red snapper gather around reefs, wrecks, and ledges. their diet includes small fish, shrimp, and squid.
ballan wrasse crush shellfish and sea urchins with strong throat teeth. thick lips and mottled colors suit rocky european reefs.
cleaner wrasses advertise with a bright stripe and dance at reef stations. larger fish wait while parasites are picked from skin and gills.
hogfish root through sand with long pig-like snouts in search of shellfish. adults can change from female to male as social groups shift.
green sea turtles graze seagrass meadows with finely serrated jaws. adults migrate long distances between feeding and nesting grounds.
hawksbill sea turtles reach into reef crevices with narrow hooked beaks. a diet rich in sponges helps shape coral communities.
leatherback sea turtles cross entire oceans while hunting jellies. a flexible ridged shell and internal heat help them enter cold water.
loggerhead sea turtles crush crabs and mollusks with massive jaws. females often return near their birth beaches to nest.
leafy seadragons drift among seaweed with elaborate skin lobes that resemble leaves. males carry eggs beneath the tail.
weedy seadragons rely on slender bodies and small leaf-like lobes for camouflage. males brood rows of eggs on the underside of the tail.
black-lip pearl oysters line their shells with dark-edged nacre. a trapped irritant can become coated in the same pearly material.
giant clams host photosynthetic algae inside brightly colored mantles. heavy shells remain anchored to one reef spot throughout adulthood.
pacific geoducks bury their shells deep while a long siphon reaches the seafloor. these clams can survive for well over a century.
queen conchs graze algae with a long flexible snout. adults develop a broad flared shell lip and move by vaulting on one muscular foot.
red abalones cling to pacific rocks with broad muscular feet. rows of shell holes release water that has passed over the gills.
bigfin reef squid hover in coordinated groups around warm reefs. shifting colors and body patterns signal to nearby squid.
colossal squid carry swiveling hooks on their arms and tentacles. enormous eyes gather faint light in the deep southern ocean.
giant squid hunt deep ocean prey with two long feeding tentacles. the largest eyes in the animal world watch for movement in darkness.
humboldt squid flash red and white while hunting in large groups. powerful beaks and grasping suckers handle fish and other squid.
ballyhoo skim warm ocean surfaces with an extended lower jaw. tight schools scatter into quick leaps when predators strike.
houndfish hunt near the surface with long jaws filled with fine teeth. powerful leaps can carry their narrow bodies far above the water.
tropical flyingfish accelerate underwater before spreading enlarged fins above the surface. glides help them escape pursuing predators.
striped bass split their lives between salt and fresh water, returning upriver to spawn. a long-lived striper may see three decades.
atlantic croakers vibrate muscles against the swim bladder to make a croaking sound. chin barbels locate worms in sandy bays.
black drum crush oysters and crabs with rounded throat teeth. large adults develop dark vertical bars that fade with age.
red drum use powerful tails to patrol surf and estuaries. one or more black spots near the tail may confuse predators about which end is the head.
striped mullet leap clear of the water and travel in coastal schools. they graze algae and detritus with specialized digestive systems.
weakfish are named for delicate mouth tissue that tears easily around a hook. iridescent spots scatter across their bronze backs.
white perch tolerate fresh and brackish water along the atlantic coast. deep silver bodies gather in schools around river mouths.
yellowfin croakers search sandy surf zones with a small chin barbel. internal muscles produce croaks and drumming calls.
black rockfish gather above reefs and kelp along the north pacific coast. like other rockfish, they give birth to live young.
black sea bass shelter around reefs, piers, and wrecks. many begin life as female and later become male.
canary rockfish glow orange-yellow over deep pacific reefs. these long-lived fish mature slowly and give birth to live young.
scup use small strong teeth to crush shellfish and other bottom prey. deep silver bodies gather around piers, reefs, and eelgrass.
sheepshead carry flat human-like front teeth for biting barnacles and crabs. dark bars cross their high silver bodies.
tautog pry mussels and crabs from rocky structure with thick lips and strong teeth. adults return to familiar shelters year after year.
yelloweye rockfish can live for more than a century on deep pacific reefs. bright golden eyes stand out against orange-red bodies.
lingcod guard rocky dens and ambush fish with a huge tooth-lined mouth. despite the name, they are greenling relatives rather than cod.
milkfish graze algae and tiny organisms in warm coastal shallows. deeply forked tails drive large schools through lagoons and estuaries.
roosterfish raise seven long dorsal spines while chasing prey through tropical surf. dark bands cross their sleek silver bodies.
atlantic tarpon gulp air with a lung-like swim bladder when coastal water runs low on oxygen. giant silver scales flash during leaps.
barramundi move between rivers and coasts and can breathe in low-oxygen water. many mature first as males and later become females.
common snook wait around mangrove roots and current seams to ambush prey. a bold black lateral line divides their silver flanks.
bonefish sweep tropical flats in silvery schools and root for buried prey. their speed and pale bodies make them difficult to follow in shallow water.
florida pompano search warm surf for crabs, clams, and sand fleas. short blunt snouts lead into deep, silvery bodies.
ladyfish race through warm shallows after schooling prey and often leap when pursued. a deeply forked tail powers their slender bodies.
permit browse tropical flats for crabs and shellfish with rubbery mouths. tall silver bodies carry long sickle-shaped dorsal and anal fins.
clown knifefish undulate one long belly fin to glide forward or backward. dark eye-like spots line their silver nocturnal bodies.
clown loaches rest in groups and make clicking sounds while feeding. orange bodies carry three broad black bands and small eye spines.
discus move through quiet amazon backwaters with round, flattened bodies. parents feed newly hatched young with nutrient-rich skin mucus.
freshwater angelfish slip between tall plants on narrow triangular bodies. long fins and vertical bars resemble stems and shadows.
giant gouramis breathe surface air through a specialized labyrinth organ. adults graze plants but also investigate insects and small animals.
nile tilapia thrive in warm lakes and rivers on a varied diet. females protect eggs and young inside their mouths.
oscars are large south american cichlids that recognize routines and defend territories. a tail eyespot may redirect attacks away from the head.
siamese fighting fish breathe surface air with a labyrinth organ. males build bubble nests and guard the eggs beneath them.
tambaqui follow seasonal floods into forests to feed on fruit and seeds. strong square teeth crack tough plant material.
walking catfish wriggle across wet ground using stiff pectoral spines for support. an air-breathing organ helps them survive the journey.
giant snakeheads breathe air and guard schools of young near the surface. long bodies launch sudden attacks from flooded vegetation.
golden dorado chase fish through powerful south american rivers. muscular tails, heavy jaws, and golden scales suit life in fast current.
golden mahseer migrate through swift mountain rivers to reach spawning grounds. large scales shine bronze beneath reddish fins.
peacock bass are aggressive south american cichlids rather than true bass. adults guard nests and hunt fish in warm clear water.
red-bellied piranhas communicate with barks and drum-like sounds. schools provide protection as they search for fish, insects, and carrion.
silver arowanas patrol the surface with upturned mouths and long bodies. powerful jumps capture insects and small animals above the water.
blue whales are the largest animals known to have lived. pleated throats expand around vast mouthfuls of water that baleen filters for krill.
common bottlenose dolphins coordinate with whistles, clicks, and body signals. echolocation reveals prey hidden in dark or cloudy water.
humpback whales use long pectoral fins while turning and feeding. males produce layered songs that change across breeding seasons.
killer whales live in close family groups with distinct calls and hunting traditions. different populations specialize in different prey.
sperm whales make deep dives to hunt squid with powerful echolocation clicks. their enormous square heads contain a waxy spermaceti organ.
